This skill takes the current conversation context and codebase understanding and produces a spec. Do NOT interview the user; just synthesize what you already know.

The issue tracker and triage label vocabulary should have been provided to you. If not, tell the user to run `/setup-matt-pocock-skills`.

## Process

1. Explore the repo to understand the current state of the codebase, if you haven't already. Use the project's domain glossary vocabulary throughout the spec, and respect any ADRs in the area you're touching.

2. Sketch out the seams at which you're going to test the feature. Existing seams should be preferred to new ones. Use the highest seam possible. If new seams are needed, propose them at the highest point you can. The fewer seams across the codebase, the better - the ideal number is one.

Check with the user that these seams match their expectations.

3. Write the spec using the template below, then publish it to the project issue tracker. Apply the `ready-for-agent` triage label - no need for additional triage.

<spec-template>

## Problem Statement

The problem that the user is facing, from the user's perspective.

## Solution

The solution to the problem, from the user's perspective.

## User Stories

A LONG, numbered list of user stories. Each user story should be in the format of:

1. As an <actor>, I want a <feature>, so that <benefit>

<user-story-example>
1. As a mobile bank customer, I want to see balance on my accounts, so that I can make better informed decisions about my spending
</user-story-example>

This list of user stories should be extremely extensive and cover all aspects of the feature.

## Implementation Decisions

A list of implementation decisions that were made. This can include:

- The modules that will be built/modified
- The interfaces of those modules that will be modified
- Technical clarifications from the developer
- Architectural decisions
- Schema changes
- API contracts
- Specific interactions

Do NOT include specific file paths or code snippets. They may end up being outdated very quickly.

Exception: if a prototype produced a snippet that encodes a decision more precisely than prose can (state machine, reducer, schema, type shape), inline it within the relevant decision and note briefly that it came from a prototype. Trim to the decision-rich parts, not a working demo, just the important bits.

## Testing Decisions

A list of testing decisions that were made. Include:

- A description of what makes a good test (only test external behavior, not implementation details)
- Which modules will be tested
- Prior art for the tests (i.e. similar types of tests in the codebase)

## Out of Scope

A description of the things that are out of scope for this spec.

## Further Notes

Any further notes about the feature.

</spec-template>

# drops

A cross-project issue tracker for AI coding agents. Go, pure-Go SQLite, and
Cobra; one database for every repository, with the project resolved from the
working directory.

**Read [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) before working here.** It carries the gate, the

# Working in drops

A cross-project issue tracker for AI coding agents. Go, pure-Go SQLite, and Cobra;
one database for every repository, with the project resolved from the working
directory.

## Agent skills

### Issue tracker

GitHub Issues on `tedkulp/drops`, driven by the `gh` CLI. See
[docs/agents/issue-tracker.md](docs/agents/issue-tracker.md); its **Wayfinding
operations** section defines how to work a map. Issues do **not** live in the
`drops` store any more — that history is closed and stays where it is.

### Triage labels

The five canonical roles, each label string equal to its name. See
[docs/agents/triage-labels.md](docs/agents/triage-labels.md).

### Domain docs

Single-context: `CONTEXT.md` at the root, ADRs under `docs/adr/` once there are
any. See [docs/agents/domain.md](docs/agents/domain.md).

### Which skill for what

`codebase-design` for package shape and seams, `tdd` for build tickets, `grilling`
plus `domain-modeling` for decision tickets.

## The gate

`just test-all`: `go vet` and a gofmt check, then `go test ./... -race`. A green
`go test` is not a green build.

CI runs this **recipe**, not a copy of it. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` installs
`just` and calls `just test-all`, because a workflow that wrote the steps out
would be a second gate free to drift from this one — and a hand-rolled `go test`
step would drop the `DROPS_DB` tripwire below without saying so. `release_test.go`
holds the workflow to the recipe. A second CI job runs `goreleaser check`, so a
broken `.goreleaser.yaml` is found on a push rather than on a tag.

The gofmt check formats what **git** counts as part of this tree — tracked files
plus untracked ones git would offer to add — and not everything under `.`. So an
unformatted `.go` file left in the gitignored `/.scratch/` does not fail the gate,
while a new file you have not run `git add` on still does. "What git counts" means
git's whole exclude set, not `.gitignore` alone: `.git/info/exclude` and your
`core.excludesFile` are read too, so the gate's view of this tree is exactly `git
status`'s view, and the untracked half of that is as machine-specific as `git
status` is. Tracked files are not — `--cached` ignores excludes.

The vet half has the mirror-image trap, and the gate now covers it. `./...` is
not every package in this tree: the go tool drops `testdata` directories from
that pattern, and any directory whose name begins with `.` or `_`. So
`internal/lockfile/testdata/holder` — the real second process the lockfile
contention tests build and run, not sample data — was formatted but never
vetted. The gate vets those packages by path, and the set is **derived** as the
directories git counts minus the ones `go list ./...` reports, rather than by
naming `testdata`, so a helper added under any skipped directory is vetted on
arrival. Directories under a nested `go.mod` are excluded, because `go vet`
refuses a path in another module and `tools/mutate/testdata/fixture` is a
deliberately-mutated corpus for the mutate tool's own tests.

`test` and `mutate` export `DROPS_DB` to `/dev/null/no-default-store-in-tests/drops.db`
— not a scratch store but a tripwire, so a test that reaches for `store.DefaultPath()`
fails with ENOTDIR and names the path. Since the cutover (`dw32p.28`) this is the
**only** thing between a test and the real store: the binary this repository builds
owns `~/.drops/drops.db`, so `internal/store`'s development guard is gone and nothing
in runtime code refuses that path any more. Issues live in the store the suite must
never open.

Four tools lie about success here:

- `gofmt -l` exits zero while listing files. The file list is the signal, never `$?`.
- `grep -c` exits one on zero matches and silently skips the rest of an `&&` chain.
- `go test` prints `ok` for a package whose tests all skipped. Read the skip count
  and the test events before treating that output as proof.
- `go run` exits 1 whatever its program exited, printing `exit status 3` to stderr.
  A recipe that needs the program's own exit code must `go build` and run the binary.

## Test discipline

The dominant defect in this codebase is a test that appears to cover a requirement
but **cannot fail for it**. Coverage does not detect it: `render` and `resolve` sit
at 100% function coverage and mutation still found defects in both. Annotated
red-checks found zero holes across the reference build; unannotated mutation found
every one.

So the standard is not a number. It is that each requirement has a **control** — the
production branch that makes it true — and that control has been mutated with the
test observed **red**.

### Which controls get mutated

One per **requirement clause**: a behavioural claim the ticket's question names. Not
one per test function — that turns the count into the goal and selects for cheap
mutations.

Where a clause is too coarse to mutate in one place, split it by **load-bearing
branch**: parsers, orderings, comparisons, conflict resolution, guards, refusals.
Those are where a wrong implementation still passes. A struct that round-trips does
not need a control; a comparator does.

### How a mutation is run

`just mutate`. The four steps are the recipe's, not yours:

1. Snapshot the file and record its checksum.
2. Apply the mutation.
3. Run the one named test, expecting failure. A pass is the finding: the test does
   not cover the clause — fix the test, not the record.
4. Restore from the snapshot and verify the checksum matches.

The snapshot is harness-owned, so **you no longer have to commit first**. `git
checkout` was never the restore here — a restore command cannot distinguish a
mutation from uncommitted work — and the harness never runs one. A run killed
between steps 2 and 4 leaves a journal naming exactly what to put back; the next
run refuses to start, and `just mutate --restore` finishes it.

Controls live beside the code they mutate, in each package's `mutations.json`: a
name, the requirement clause it proves, the file, the `old` → `new` edit, and the
test. `just mutate` runs every one; `just mutate core` scopes to a package or a
single control name; `--list` prints what is catalogued without running it; and
`--file/--old/--new/--test/--clause` runs one ad hoc, for while you are still
finding out whether a test can fail at all.

It refuses more than it accepts, and every refusal is a finding, never a pass:

| It says | It means |
|---|---|
| `GREEN` | the test passed with the branch broken, so it does not cover the clause |
| `NOT RUN` | no test of that name ran — `go test -run` matching nothing prints `ok` and exits 0 |
| `BUILD FAILED` | the mutation does not compile, so it proves nothing about the test |
| `NO MATCH` | `old` is absent or appears twice; a mutation must name exactly one branch |
| `BASELINE RED` | the test was already failing, so its red says nothing |

Exit 0 means every control went red, 1 that there is a finding, 2 that it was
called wrong, and **3 that a restore failed and the tree may still hold a
mutation**.

`just mutate` is deliberately not part of `test-all`. The gate asks whether this
commit is green; mutation asks whether the suite can fail, and pays a compile per
control to answer. Run it when a ticket adds or changes a control.

### What a ticket records

Enumerate, in `close --reason`: each control (file and behaviour), the test that went
red, and confirmation of the restore. `just mutate <package>` prints exactly that, so
the enumeration is a by-product rather than prose written from memory, and `--json` is
the same record for a machine. A bare count is unauditable — it is the form that let a
ticket record "one control" without anyone reading it as "one".

A control that is not in a `mutations.json` was proved once and can never be proved
again. Catalogue it.

### Seams

**Discovered facts become constructor parameters; real subsystems stay real.**

A fact a process learns about its environment — the writer, terminal-ness, measured
width, the pager, the clock, the ID source — is a struct field passed in, never
discovered at the point of use. `render` accepts all four of its environment facts,
so its whole suite is byte-exact literals with no fake anywhere; the reference build
discovered them and needed two package-level variables to make the same behaviour
reachable.

The datastore is not such a fact. There is deliberately no `Store` interface: every
test runs against real temp SQLite, real git, and real `flock`. `synctest` cannot
fake SQLite's busy-handler sleep, so lock-contention tests are real-clock. Making
these fakeable would trade a real defect class for a faster suite.

### Serialized contracts

For at least one case per serialized contract, run the real writer and decode its
bytes. Deriving both sides from the same description tests the description.

### The CLI is a contract

`docs/cli-contract.md` is what agents read to drive drops. A verb that
changes shape without that file changing is a defect.

Every command in the tree carries at least one boundary test through
`RunForTest(args, db, cwd)`, asserting what the doc says a reader observes: a
byte-exact row for a scanning verb, the JSON shape for a reading verb, the store
effect for a mutating verb. A census test walks the command tree and fails on any
command absent from the tested-verb registry, so skipping one is an edit to a visible
list rather than an omission.

## Changelog

`CHANGELOG.md` follows Keep a Changelog. Every change made after the latest
release goes under `## [Unreleased]` (create it when absent), grouped under the
appropriate change category. Only release work moves those entries into a dated
version section.

## Lessons retained from the reference build

- Re-check the premise before the next round of rigour, not after it.
- Measure before changing a documented fact. A confidently wrong count is worse than
  a stale one.

## Planning

This repository has no `.internal/` tree. Durable research belongs in `docs/`; live
plans and decisions belong in the issue tracker. The local `.gitignore` deliberately
overrides the workstation's global `.internal/` exclusion so accidental files cannot
disappear from status.
# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues in
[`tedkulp/drops`](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops). Use the `gh` CLI for all
operations; run it inside a clone and it infers the repo from `git remote -v`.

> **This repo builds a tracker but does not use it as one.** Until 2026-09-06 the
> issues for this repo lived in `drops` itself. That history — 79 closed issues,
> including the `dw32p` rewrite map — stays in `~/.drops/drops.db` under the
> `drops` project and is not migrated; the `dw32p.N` ids cited in `CHANGELOG.md`
> and `docs/research/*.md` refer to it. Nothing is open there. For how the
> product's own CLI behaves, see [docs/cli-contract.md](../cli-contract.md).

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --comments`, filtering comments by `jq` and also fetching labels.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number> --comments` and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh pr list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,author,authorAssociation,comments` then keep only `authorAssociation` of `CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR`, or `NONE` (drop `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR`).
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Run `gh issue view <number> --comments`.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (`gh api` on the sub-issues endpoint). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). GitHub reports `issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (`issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0`, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

vetted. The gate vets those packages by path, and the set is **derived** as the
directories git counts minus the ones `go list ./...` reports, rather than by
naming `testdata`, so a helper added under any skipped directory is vetted on
arrival. Directories under a nested `go.mod` are excluded, because `go vet`
refuses a path in another module and `tools/mutate/testdata/fixture` is a
deliberately-mutated corpus for the mutate tool's own tests.

`test` and `mutate` export `DROPS_DB` to `/dev/null/no-default-store-in-tests/drops.db`
— not a scratch store but a tripwire, so a test that reaches for `store.DefaultPath()`
fails with ENOTDIR and names the path. Since the cutover (`dw32p.28`) this is the
**only** thing between a test and the real store: the binary this repository builds
owns `~/.drops/drops.db`, so `internal/store`'s development guard is gone and nothing
in runtime code refuses that path any more. Issues live in the store the suite must
never open.

Four tools lie about success here:

- `gofmt -l` exits zero while listing files. The file list is the signal, never `$?`.
- `grep -c` exits one on zero matches and silently skips the rest of an `&&` chain.
- `go test` prints `ok` for a package whose tests all skipped. Read the skip count
  and the test events before treating that output as proof.
- `go run` exits 1 whatever its program exited, printing `exit status 3` to stderr.
  A recipe that needs the program's own exit code must `go build` and run the binary.

## Test discipline

The dominant defect in this codebase is a test that appears to cover a requirement
but **cannot fail for it**. Coverage does not detect it: `render` and `resolve` sit
at 100% function coverage and mutation still found defects in both. Annotated
red-checks found zero holes across the reference build; unannotated mutation found
every one.

So the standard is not a number. It is that each requirement has a **control** — the
production branch that makes it true — and that control has been mutated with the
test observed **red**.

### Which controls get mutated

One per **requirement clause**: a behavioural claim the ticket's question names. Not
one per test function — that turns the count into the goal and selects for cheap
mutations.

Where a clause is too coarse to mutate in one place, split it by **load-bearing
branch**: parsers, orderings, comparisons, conflict resolution, guards, refusals.
Those are where a wrong implementation still passes. A struct that round-trips does
not need a control; a comparator does.

### How a mutation is run

`just mutate`. The four steps are the recipe's, not yours:

1. Snapshot the file and record its checksum.
2. Apply the mutation.
3. Run the one named test, expecting failure. A pass is the finding: the test does
   not cover the clause — fix the test, not the record.
4. Restore from the snapshot and verify the checksum matches.

The snapshot is harness-owned, so **you no longer have to commit first**. `git
checkout` was never the restore here — a restore command cannot distinguish a
mutation from uncommitted work — and the harness never runs one. A run killed
between steps 2 and 4 leaves a journal naming exactly what to put back; the next
run refuses to start, and `just mutate --restore` finishes it.

Controls live beside the code they mutate, in each package's `mutations.json`: a
name, the requirement clause it proves, the file, the `old` → `new` edit, and the
test. `just mutate` runs every one; `just mutate core` scopes to a package or a
single control name; `--list` prints what is catalogued without running it; and
`--file/--old/--new/--test/--clause` runs one ad hoc, for while you are still
finding out whether a test can fail at all.

It refuses more than it accepts, and every refusal is a finding, never a pass:

| It says | It means |
|---|---|
| `GREEN` | the test passed with the branch broken, so it does not cover the clause |
| `NOT RUN` | no test of that name ran — `go test -run` matching nothing prints `ok` and exits 0 |
| `BUILD FAILED` | the mutation does not compile, so it proves nothing about the test |
| `NO MATCH` | `old` is absent or appears twice; a mutation must name exactly one branch |
| `BASELINE RED` | the test was already failing, so its red says nothing |

Exit 0 means every control went red, 1 that there is a finding, 2 that it was
called wrong, and **3 that a restore failed and the tree may still hold a
mutation**.

`just mutate` is deliberately not part of `test-all`. The gate asks whether this
commit is green; mutation asks whether the suite can fail, and pays a compile per
control to answer. Run it when a ticket adds or changes a control.

### What a ticket records

Enumerate, in `close --reason`: each control (file and behaviour), the test that went
red, and confirmation of the restore. `just mutate <package>` prints exactly that, so
the enumeration is a by-product rather than prose written from memory, and `--json` is
the same record for a machine. A bare count is unauditable — it is the form that let a
ticket record "one control" without anyone reading it as "one".

A control that is not in a `mutations.json` was proved once and can never be proved
again. Catalogue it.

### Seams

**Discovered facts become constructor parameters; real subsystems stay real.**

A fact a process learns about its environment — the writer, terminal-ness, measured
width, the pager, the clock, the ID source — is a struct field passed in, never
discovered at the point of use. `render` accepts all four of its environment facts,
so its whole suite is byte-exact literals with no fake anywhere; the reference build
discovered them and needed two package-level variables to make the same behaviour
reachable.

The datastore is not such a fact. There is deliberately no `Store` interface: every
test runs against real temp SQLite, real git, and real `flock`. `synctest` cannot
fake SQLite's busy-handler sleep, so lock-contention tests are real-clock. Making
these fakeable would trade a real defect class for a faster suite.

### Serialized contracts

For at least one case per serialized contract, run the real writer and decode its
bytes. Deriving both sides from the same description tests the description.

### The CLI is a contract

`docs/cli-contract.md` is what agents read to drive drops. A verb that
changes shape without that file changing is a defect.

Every command in the tree carries at least one boundary test through
`RunForTest(args, db, cwd)`, asserting what the doc says a reader observes: a
byte-exact row for a scanning verb, the JSON shape for a reading verb, the store
effect for a mutating verb. A census test walks the command tree and fails on any
command absent from the tested-verb registry, so skipping one is an edit to a visible
list rather than an omission.

## Changelog

`CHANGELOG.md` follows Keep a Changelog. Every change made after the latest
release goes under `## [Unreleased]` (create it when absent), grouped under the
appropriate change category. Only release work moves those entries into a dated
version section.

## Lessons retained from the reference build

- Re-check the premise before the next round of rigour, not after it.
- Measure before changing a documented fact. A confidently wrong count is worse than
  a stale one.

## Planning

This repository has no `.internal/` tree. Durable research belongs in `docs/`; live
plans and decisions belong in the issue tracker. The local `.gitignore` deliberately
overrides the workstation's global `.internal/` exclusion so accidental files cannot
disappear from status.
# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues in
[`tedkulp/drops`](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops). Use the `gh` CLI for all
operations; run it inside a clone and it infers the repo from `git remote -v`.

> **This repo builds a tracker but does not use it as one.** Until 2026-09-06 the
> issues for this repo lived in `drops` itself. That history — 79 closed issues,
> including the `dw32p` rewrite map — stays in `~/.drops/drops.db` under the
> `drops` project and is not migrated; the `dw32p.N` ids cited in `CHANGELOG.md`
> and `docs/research/*.md` refer to it. Nothing is open there. For how the
> product's own CLI behaves, see [docs/cli-contract.md](../cli-contract.md).

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --comments`, filtering comments by `jq` and also fetching labels.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: `gh issue close <number> --comment "..."`

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

- **Read a PR**: `gh pr view <number> --comments` and `gh pr diff <number>` for the diff.
- **List external PRs for triage**: `gh pr list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,author,authorAssociation,comments` then keep only `authorAssociation` of `CONTRIBUTOR`, `FIRST_TIME_CONTRIBUTOR`, or `NONE` (drop `OWNER`/`MEMBER`/`COLLABORATOR`).
- **Comment / label / close**: `gh pr comment`, `gh pr edit --add-label`/`--remove-label`, `gh pr close`.

GitHub shares one number space across issues and PRs, so a bare `#42` may be either: resolve with `gh pr view 42` and fall back to `gh issue view 42`.

## When a skill says "publish to the issue tracker"

Create a GitHub issue.

## When a skill says "fetch the relevant ticket"

Run `gh issue view <number> --comments`.

## Wayfinding operations

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.

- **Map**: a single issue labelled `wayfinder:map`, holding the Notes / Decisions-so-far / Fog body. `gh issue create --label wayfinder:map`.
- **Child ticket**: an issue linked to the map as a GitHub sub-issue (`gh api` on the sub-issues endpoint). Where sub-issues aren't enabled, add the child to a task list in the map body and put `Part of #<map>` at the top of the child body. Labels: `wayfinder:<type>` (`research`/`prototype`/`grilling`/`task`). Once claimed, the ticket is assigned to the driving dev.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). GitHub reports `issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only, the live gate). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Frontier query**: list the map's open children (`gh issue list --state open`, scoped to the map's sub-issues / task list), drop any with an open blocker (`issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by > 0`, or an open issue in the `Blocked by` line) or an assignee; first in map order wins.
- **Claim**: `gh issue edit <n> --add-assignee @me`, the session's first write.
- **Resolve**: `gh issue comment <n> --body "<answer>"`, then `gh issue close <n>`, then append a context pointer (gist + link) to the map's Decisions-so-far.

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

{"body":"## Destination

A spec for board v1 in `drops tui`, sharp enough to hand to `/to-tickets`, with every core prerequisite it needs identified and ticketed ahead of the TUI work.

## Notes

- Domain: `internal/tui` (read its `doc.go` first — the refresh/poll model, the follow stack, and why the detail pane is opaque), `internal/core` reads and writes, `CONTEXT.md` (**Board column**, Ready/Blocked issue, Deferral).
- Skills: `grilling` + `domain-modeling` for decision tickets; `codebase-design` wherever a new core read or write is shaped; `prototype` for how it looks.
- Reference: bv (beads_viewer) board — `b` opens it; columns Open | In Progress | Blocked | Closed from *stored* status; cards ordered priority then created; 4-line cards (type, P, id, age / title / assignee, blockers, downstream, label count / labels); no card moves.
- Settled while charting (2026-09-15), standing for every ticket:
  - **Columns** are derived (see **Board column** in `CONTEXT.md`): Ready | Blocked | In progress | Closed. An in-progress issue that is blocked stays in In progress with a marker.
  - **Home**: a mode inside `drops tui` that replaces the left pane; the detail pane, follow, `x`, `y`, and the stale marker carry over. Not a separate command.
  - **Card moves** change status. For claims, the close reason, reopening, and refusals, see the decision on moves below.
  - **Order within a column** is the CLI's (priority, newest, id) — no manual ranking. **Closed** is always shown, most recently closed first.
  - **Labels** show on cards, which needs a bulk label read in core (the TUI may not read per card).
- Data-wise, already in place: stored status, priority, type, assignee, created/started/closed timestamps, deferral, `core.OpenBlockers` (blocked counts in one read), `core.UnblockImpacts` (downstream counts), `core.SetIssueStatus`, claim/release.

## Decisions so far

- [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3): moving into In progress claims when unclaimed, in one new transactional core write; nothing releases; closing uses the `x close` `$EDITOR` flow (empty reason cancels); leaving Closed asks the `reopen` y/N; Ready and Blocked both mean `open`; no revision guard.
- [How does the board fit the navigator's keymap and refresh model?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/5): `B` toggles the board (no flag, not an `Esc` layer), and cursor, filter, `a`, `r`, and follow trail carry over; `tab`/`shift+tab` moves between columns and every existing key keeps its meaning; `m` opens an `open`/`in progress`/`closed` picker; `r` is the same predicate, which empties Blocked; `C` only shows a notice; the cursor rides its id and otherwise moves to the next card; polling is unchanged.
- [How does the board look: columns, cards, and the detail pane?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/2): paged columns — the detail pane keeps 40% (min 38), columns never go under 28 wide and scroll sideways keeping the focused one on screen (1 at 80 cols, 2 at 120, 4 at 200); 3-line cards (mark/P/type/id/age · title · assignee/blocked by/unblocks/labels); columns scroll by card with a `39–41` range in the heading; empty columns show a dim hint. Prototype on branch `prototype/board-look`.
- [What reads does the board make, and which does core lack?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/4): four reads per refresh — the existing open/in-progress list; a new core read of closed issues in scope, store-ordered `closed_at DESC, id`, no limit in v1; blocked-by and unblocks counts from one blocker-graph read (core change so impacts don't re-read `OpenBlockers`); a new store-wide live-labels map. 8.8ms on a 1,031-issue store, inside the refresh budget.
- [What does the board's contract and test surface look like?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/6): a `### The board` subsection in the contract's navigator section, plus `B`, `tab` and `m` in the key table and help; outside that, only a Known rough edges line about Closed having no limit; tests check model state, store effect for every `m` flow, frames only for width, and card lines byte-exact; controls go only on branches the board owns (12 TUI groups) plus core controls on start-and-claim, the closed read, live labels, and the blocker graph.

## Not yet specified

- **Scaling past the corpus.** At 10k closed issues a board refresh is ~105ms, and the cost is in `OpenBlockers`: it reads every full issue row to learn which issues are terminal, so the list pays the same. Not a v1 prerequisite; revisit if a real store grows that large. See [What reads does the board make, and which does core lack?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/4).

## Out of scope

- **Grouping modes** (bv's `s`: priority or type columns): not v1. No new data is needed, so it's a TUI-only follow-up effort once v1 exists.
- **Manual ordering within a column**: needs a rank column (schema v8) and a sync merge rule for a new replicated record; priority already acts as the rank.
- **Custom workflow stages** (review, QA): a change to the three-status model that readiness and sync depend on; its own effort if ever.
- **A separate `drops board` command**: the board lives inside `drops tui`.
- **A CLI verb for the start-and-claim write** (e.g. `drops start`): it would change the agent-facing CLI contract, which is beyond the board spec. See [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3).
- **A test holding the `?` help screen to the contract's key table**: a new doc-sync test for the whole navigator, not something the board needs; its own ticket if wanted. See [What does the board's contract and test surface look like?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/6).

# Glossary

## Project

A logical namespace for issues and memories that can exist in more than one store. A project keeps its identity when its human-facing name or repository locations change.

## Project key

The immutable, opaque identity of a project across stores and machines.

## Replica

An exclusive, monotonic lineage of a writable drops store. Processes share a replica only when they operate on the same serialized store; a copy that can be written independently is a different replica.

## Replica key

The immutable, opaque identity of one replica. A replica key orders concurrent record revisions and distinguishes an update from an identifier collision; it is not a project or machine identity.

## Project slug

The human-facing name used to address a project. A slug is unique within a store but is not the project's identity; renaming a project changes its slug without changing its project key.

## Workspace binding

A machine-local association between an existing, canonical absolute directory and a project key. A project can have multiple workspace bindings, but a path names at most one project. A Git-backed binding uses the main repository root so linked worktrees share it. Workspace bindings are not part of the project and do not cross stores or machines.

## Repository locator

A normalized, machine-independent Git remote name used to discover a project from an unbound checkout. A project can have multiple repository locators. A locator is evidence for association, not project identity.

## Reserved project

One of the built-in `global` or `inbox` projects. Each has a well-known project key and a fixed slug and role, so independently created stores converge on the same identity. Reserved projects cannot be renamed or archived.

## Memory

A durable notebook entry that an agent explicitly writes, lists, searches, shows, or edits. Every memory belongs to one project, but a search can span projects. A memory has a permanent opaque identity; it is not ranked or injected into a session automatically.

## Memory provenance

An optional free-text description of where a memory's knowledge came from, such as a skill, document, or migration. Provenance is independent of the project that owns the memory.

## Memory supersession

The replacement of one memory by another while preserving the old memory and its permanent identity. Superseded memories remain directly addressable but are absent from ordinary lists and searches.

## Replicated record

An atomic unit of state merged between stores. An issue, memory, or project is one replicated record; each label membership, dependency, comment, repository locator, and issue-parent relation is another. Concurrent changes do not merge individual fields within a record.

## Record revision

The generation and replica key attached to a replicated record. The generation advances from the version a writer observed; the replica key makes concurrent revisions deterministic without treating wall-clock time as authority.

## Tombstone

The versioned state that records an explicit removal. A tombstone participates in conflict resolution and preserves identity; absence from a mirror never means deletion.

## Issue parent

The single explicit parent relation of an issue. Parentage is independent of the issue's opaque ID, even when newly minted child IDs include their parent's ID for readability.

## ID ownership

The permanent reservation of one opaque ID to either an issue or a memory. Ownership survives tombstoning, so an ID can never change kind or be reused.

## Replica succession

The recorded replacement of one active replica key by another in the same store lineage. Succession affects future authorship only; it never rewrites existing record revisions or creation origins.

## Live issue

An issue that has not been tombstoned, whatever its status. Liveness is independent of whether an issue is open or closed: a closed issue is live, a tombstoned one is not.

## Open issue

A live issue whose status is `open` or `in_progress`. Being open is a claim about whether the work is finished, not about whether it has started, so an issue someone is part-way through is open.

## Ready issue

An open issue with no blocking dependency on another issue that is itself unfinished. Readiness is computed from the dependency graph rather than stored, so it changes when a blocker's status changes and never needs to be maintained.

## Blocked issue

An open issue with at least one blocking dependency on an unfinished issue. Blocked and ready are complementary properties of the same open set; neither is a status an issue can be put into.

## Board column

One of the four groupings a board places a live issue in: Ready, Blocked, In progress, or Closed. A column is derived, never stored: an `open` issue sits in Ready or Blocked by its readiness, an `in_progress` issue sits in In progress whether or not it is blocked, and a `closed` issue sits in Closed. Because Ready and Blocked are properties rather than statuses, an issue cannot be put into either; it arrives there by being open.

## Related dependency

A non-blocking association between two issues. `A related B` is undirected to a reader even though its replicated record has `from` and `to` fields: A and B each read the other under `Related`, and neither end implies origin or precedence.

## Discovered-from dependency

A directed provenance relation between two issues. `A discovered-from B` means A was discovered or derived from B: A reads B under `Discovered from`, while B reads A under `Discovered`.

## Deferral

The convention of marking an issue as deliberately postponed. Deferral is expressed as an ordinary label and carries no meaning to the model: a deferred issue is an ordinary open issue, and nothing computes readiness or ordering differently because of it.

=================== #2
# How does the board look: columns, cards, and the detail pane?
labels: wayfinder:prototype

## Question

What does board v1 look like on screen? Specifically:

- What a **card** shows, and in how many lines (bv uses four: type/priority/id/age, title, assignee/blockers/downstream/label count, labels). Which of those earn their space here — and how the blocked marker on an In progress card reads.
- How **four columns plus the detail pane** fit the widths people actually run at (80, 120, 200+ columns): do columns shrink, scroll horizontally, collapse to one focused column, or does the detail pane yield?
- How a column that is **longer than the screen** scrolls (Closed especially), and how an empty column renders (Closed is always shown, so collapsing empties is not automatic).

Resolve with a throwaway prototype rendered against a real store; link it as an asset.


--- COMMENTS ---
Context from [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3): there is no inline close-reason modal to design. Closing from the board reuses the `x close` `$EDITOR` flow.

--- next comment ---

Context from [How does the board fit the navigator's keymap and refresh model?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/5): these affect what the board renders.
- The board is toggled with `B`.
- `tab`/`shift+tab` moves between columns, so the layout needs a visible focused column.
- `m` opens an `x`-style picker (`open` / `in progress` / `closed`) for moving a card.
- Under `r`, Blocked renders empty with the hint `r to show blocked`.
- `C` on the board only shows a one-key notice.
- Detail-pane keys (`h` `l` `w` `enter` etc.) all keep working, so the detail pane stays on screen in board mode.

--- next comment ---

## Resolution

Picked from a throwaway prototype: **variant E, paged columns, with 3-line cards.**

Prototype, the primary source: branch [`prototype/board-look`](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/tree/prototype/board-look) (`1e0cd38`). Run it with `just board-prototype` on that branch. `[` `]` switch between the five layouts that were compared (shrink, accordion, stacked, grouped, paged), `d` sets card lines, `<` `>` force 80/120/200 columns. There was no real store on the machine it was built on, so it seeds `.scratch/PROTOTYPE-board-wipe-me.db` through core's write path (28 live issues, 300 closed); `-db <path>` points it at a real one.

**Layout: columns keep a minimum width and the board scrolls sideways**
- The detail pane stays on screen and takes 40% of the frame (at least 38 columns). The board gets the rest.
- A column is never narrower than 28 columns. As many columns as fit are shown: 1 at 80 columns, 2 at 120, all 4 at 200.
- The focused column is always on screen. `tab`/`shift+tab` scroll the board when the target is off screen.
- The board border says what is hidden on each side, e.g. `◀ 1 · 1 ▶`.
- Rejected: squeezing four columns into the list's half (unreadable below ~200 columns), focused-wide plus strips (strips are 3 columns at 80), board above the detail pane (3 cards per column at 120), and a grouped list (300 closed cards made it 991 lines).

**Card: 3 lines**
1. Status mark, `P<n>`, type, id, with age right-aligned (since created / started / closed, by column).
2. Title, cut with an ellipsis.
3. `@assignee · blocked by N · unblocks N · #label #label`, each part only when present, cut to fit.
- A blocked In progress card says so with `blocked by N` on line 3.
- bv's 4th line (labels alone) was dropped: it repeats line 3.
- Cards are separated by one blank line; the focused card is reverse video.

**Long and empty columns**
- A column scrolls a card at a time, keeping the cursor's card on screen. When it overflows, its heading shows the range: `Closed 300 · 39–41`. The focused column's heading is marked `▸`.
- An empty column keeps its heading and shows a dim hint: `none`, `nothing closed` for Closed, and `r to show blocked` for Blocked under `r`.

=================== #3
# What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?
labels: wayfinder:grilling

## Question

A card move changes status. What else does it do, and what may it refuse?

- **Claims.** Today claiming never changes status and status never changes the claim. Does moving into In progress claim for the current author when unclaimed? Does moving back out release? (Options at charting: status only; claim on entering In progress; claim and release both ways.)
- **Into Closed.** A modal asks for the close reason and ESC cancels, returning the card to its previous column. Is an empty reason allowed? Does closing touch the claim?
- **Out of Closed.** Reopening destroys `close_reason` (`SetIssueStatus` nils it); the navigator's `x` reopen confirms with the size of what's lost. Does a board move do the same?
- **Into Ready or Blocked.** Both are derived: a move "to Ready" is a move to `open`, and the card may land in Blocked instead. Are both columns valid targets, or is there one "open" target?
- **Refusals.** Tombstoned issues, a claim held by someone else, a write that loses a concurrent revision.
- **Core.** Does the answer need a new transactional core call (status + claim in one revision), or do existing calls suffice?


--- COMMENTS ---
## Resolution

A card move changes status. Each case below says what else the move does and what it may refuse.

**Into In progress**
- If nobody holds the claim, the move claims the card for the current author. An existing claim, whoever holds it, stays as it is and does not block the move.
- This happens in **one new core write**: set `in_progress` (setting `started_at` only the first time) and claim only if unclaimed, in one transaction with one revision. It never refuses because someone else holds the claim, and it keeps core's refusal of tombstoned issues. Its `internal/core/mutations.json` controls: the claim happens only when unclaimed, an existing claim is left alone, `started_at` is set only once, and a tombstoned issue is refused.
- Moving out of In progress **never releases** the claim. `x release` still does that.

**Into Closed**
- Uses the **same `$EDITOR` flow as `x close`**, not an inline text box. An empty or whitespace-only reason, or a non-zero editor exit (`:cq`), cancels, and the card goes back to its previous column. No empty reasons.
- Closing **does not touch the claim**, because the claim on closed work records who resolved it.
- Uses `SetIssueStatus(closed, reason)` as it is.

**Out of Closed** (to Ready, Blocked, or In progress)
- Asks with the **same y/N prompt as `reopen`**, which states how many characters of close reason will be lost. Any answer but `y` leaves the card in Closed. If there's no close reason, there's no prompt.
- Moving from Closed to In progress asks the same question, then follows the In progress rule above.

**Into Ready or Blocked**
- **Both columns accept a card and both mean `open`** (`SetIssueStatus(open)`). The card lands in whichever column its readiness puts it. When that isn't the column you aimed at, a status line says why (e.g. "open — blocked by 2").

**Refusals and races**
- No revision guard against what the board last displayed. Last write wins at transaction time, the same as every `x` write, and the poll plus the stale marker cover staleness.
- Tombstoned issues never show on the board. Core's existing tombstone refusal covers a mid-view race.
- A claim held by someone else never refuses a move.

**Core**
- One new transactional write for moving into In progress, as above. Every other move uses `SetIssueStatus` unchanged. Its exact name and signature are left to the build ticket (`codebase-design`).
- **No CLI verb** for it in this effort (ruled out of scope on the map).

# What reads does the board make, and which does core lack?
labels: wayfinder:grilling

## Question

Given what a card shows, what does one board refresh read, and what must core add?

- **Labels**: core exposes only per-issue `IssueLabels`; the store has an all-labels read. Shape of the bulk read (scoped by project? live only? returned as a map by issue?) and its controls.
- **Downstream counts**, if cards show them: `core.UnblockImpacts` cost against the 1025-issue corpus, next to `OpenBlockers`' 5.24ms.
- **Closed's recency order**: `tui/doc.go` says rows are in the CLI's order and never re-sorted. Does Closed get a store-ordered read by `closed_at`, or is a local sort an accepted exception?
- **Loading every closed issue** in scope: measure a board refresh including Closed, and decide whether it needs bounding.
- Whether the whole refresh stays within the poll/refresh split `tui/doc.go` measures.


--- COMMENTS ---
## Resolution

A board refresh makes **four core reads**, and core needs **three changes** before the TUI work. The measurements below come from a throwaway benchmark over scratch stores seeded through core's write path. The 1,025-issue corpus isn't on the machine that ran it, so a 1,031-issue store (1,000 closed) stood in for it.

| read | 1,031 issues | 10,031 issues (10k closed) |
|---|---|---|
| `Issues`, open + in progress, scoped | 0.15ms | 0.15ms |
| `Issues` including closed, scoped | 4.2ms | 54ms |
| `OpenBlockers` | 4.1ms | 48ms |
| `UnblockImpacts` (calls `OpenBlockers` again) | 3.9ms | 47ms |
| `store.Labels()` (all memberships, tombstoned included) | 0.33ms | 3.2ms |
| local sort of Closed by `closed_at` | 2.5ms | 36ms |
| **whole board refresh** | **8.8ms** | **105ms** |

**The reads in one refresh**
1. **Open and in-progress issues in scope.** This is the existing `Issues` read, in the CLI's order, unchanged.
2. **Closed issues in scope.** A **new core read**, ordered by `closed_at DESC, id` in the store. The TUI still never re-sorts rows; this read orders them. It has **no limit in v1**: Closed is always shown, and 8.8ms for the whole refresh sits inside the refresh budget `tui/doc.go` measures. Because the read is separate, a limit later is a one-parameter change.
3. **Blocker counts and downstream counts from one blocker graph read.** A **core change** computes unblock impacts from a blocker map the caller already has, so a refresh never pays for `OpenBlockers` twice. For example, one read returns both, or `UnblockImpacts` takes the map. The TUI doesn't count them itself, so the "only this blocker" rule stays in core. The build ticket picks the exact shape with `codebase-design`.
4. **Live labels across the whole store.** A **new core read** that returns `map[id][]name`, names sorted, one call per refresh, with no scope, the same way `OpenBlockers` works. It sits on its own live-only store query, not a filter over the export read `Labels()`. Mutation controls: a tombstoned membership is left out, and names come back in order.

**Does it fit the poll/refresh split?** Yes. The poll still reads only `write_seq`. On the real corpus a board refresh costs about the same as today's all-projects list (10ms).

**Scaling beyond the corpus is not a v1 prerequisite.** At 10k closed issues the cost is in `OpenBlockers`, not in loading Closed. It reads every full issue row just to learn which issues are terminal, so the plain list already pays that cost on a large store. This goes into the map's fog, not onto the board's route.

# How does the board fit the navigator's keymap and refresh model?
labels: wayfinder:grilling

## Question

How does the board mode behave as part of `drops tui`?

- **Entering and leaving**: which key (bv uses `b`), and what survives the switch — cursor issue, filter, `r`, `a` scope, follow stack.
- **Movement**: `h`/`l` already scroll the detail pane horizontally; what moves between columns, what moves within one, and what the card-move keys are.
- **Existing narrowings**: what `/` filter and `r` (ready-only) mean on a board — does `r` hide the Blocked column? Is `C` meaningless now that Closed always shows?
- **After a write or refresh**: the cursor rides its tracked id — including into another column after a move — and how ESC-cancelled close restores position.
- **Stale marker and polling**: unchanged, or does a board need anything different?


--- COMMENTS ---
Context from [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3): closing a card uses the `x close` `$EDITOR` flow, not an inline modal, so "ESC-cancelled close" here means an empty reason or `:cq`, and the card goes back to its previous column. Leaving Closed puts up the `reopen` y/N prompt, and a "no" leaves the card in Closed. A move to open can land in Blocked instead of Ready, so the cursor should follow the card's id to whichever column it actually lands in.

--- next comment ---

## Resolution

Board mode inside `drops tui` reuses the navigator's keymap wherever it can. Every existing key keeps its meaning in both modes, with one exception: `C` on the board.

**Entering and leaving**
- `B` toggles between the list and the board. `b` keeps paging the detail pane up.
- `drops tui` always opens in the list. There is **no `--board` flag** in v1.
- **What carries over when you switch**: the cursor's issue id, the `/` filter, `a` scope, `r`, and the follow trail. Switching reads nothing; both views use the loaded rows. The one exception is that the board always includes closed issues (see `C` below).
- `Esc` does **not** leave the board. The board is a view with its own toggle key, like `a`, and not a layer that `Esc` pops.

**Movement**
- Within a column: `j` `k` `↓` `↑` `g` `G` `^d` `^u`.
- Between columns: `tab` / `shift+tab`, cycling through the four. The cursor lands on the card nearest its old row position.
- `h` `l` `←` `→` `0` `$` `J` `K` `space` `b` `w` `enter` `f` `Backspace` `x` `y` all work on the board as they do in the list. Moving the card cursor clears the follow trail, as moving the list cursor does.

**Card moves**
- `m` opens a picker, built like the `x` modal, over the target statuses other than the card's own: `open`, `in progress`, `closed`. Ready and Blocked appear as **one `open` row**. That is how this ticket applies [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3)'s "both columns accept a card": the card lands wherever its readiness puts it, and the status line says why (e.g. "open — blocked by 2").
- The picker then runs the flows that ticket decided: `in progress` claims if unclaimed; `closed` opens the `$EDITOR` flow; leaving Closed asks `reopen`'s y/N.

**Narrowings**
- `/` filters cards in every column, unchanged.
- `r` uses the **same predicate in the same function** (`blockedBy == 0` in `applyFilter`). On the board, Blocked goes empty and shows `r to show blocked`, and blocked In progress cards are hidden too.
- `C` on the board changes nothing and shows the notice `closed always shown on the board`, which clears on the next key, like `y`'s. The board loads closed issues whatever `C` is set to, and the list keeps its own `C` state for when you switch back.

**After a write or refresh**
- The cursor follows its tracked id into whichever column the card lands in.
- A cancelled close (empty reason or `:cq`) or a "no" to reopen writes nothing, so the cursor and card stay where they were.
- If the card leaves the view (tombstoned, filtered out, or hidden by `r` after landing in Blocked), the cursor goes to the next card in the same column, or the previous card if it was the last. If the column is now empty, it goes to the nearest non-empty column. The detail pane then opens the new issue at line 0, following the existing different-issue rule.

**Stale marker and polling**
- No change: the `write_seq` poll runs every 2 seconds, `stale · R` appears on the footer, and `R` refreshes whichever view is up.

# What does the board's contract and test surface look like?
labels: wayfinder:grilling

## Question

With the look, keymap, moves, and reads decided, what does the board add to the documented contract and to the test surface?

- **Contract**: what `docs/cli-contract.md`'s TUI section says about board mode. That covers `B`, the columns and how they're derived, the card, `m` and its flows, `C`'s notice, and `r` emptying Blocked. It also covers whether anything outside the TUI section changes (no new CLI verb, per the map).
- **Boundary tests**: which observable board behaviours get a test against real temp SQLite, and at what level: a frame rendered at a fixed size, the model's state after key messages, or the store effect of a move.
- **Mutation controls**: the load-bearing branches that each need a catalogued control in `internal/tui/mutations.json` and `internal/core/mutations.json`. On the TUI side that includes column derivation (in-progress-and-blocked stays in In progress), the Closed recency order, cursor landing after a move, the cancelled-close and declined-reopen no-ops, and paging the focused column into view. On the core side it covers the new reads and the start-and-claim write decided in [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3) and [What reads does the board make, and which does core lack?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/4).


--- COMMENTS ---
## Resolution

**Contract (`docs/cli-contract.md`)**
- Board mode goes in a new `### The board` subsection at the end of "The navigator: `drops tui`". It adds a `B` row to the key table and one sentence in the intro saying the navigator has two views. The subsection says once that every key keeps its meaning, then lists the exceptions: the derived columns, the 3-line card, `tab`, `m` and its three flows, `C`'s notice, `r` emptying Blocked, where the cursor lands after a write, and paging.
- The rest of the section stays as it is. The `?` help screen and the key table both gain `B`, `tab`, and `m`.
- Outside the TUI section, only **Known rough edges** gets a line: Closed loads with no limit, and a refresh costs about 100ms at around 10k closed issues. No new verb or flag, no census change (`tui` is already registered), and no new exit code. A `CHANGELOG` entry goes under Unreleased → Added.

**Test levels** (all against real temp SQLite)
- **Model state after key messages**: column membership, focused and first visible column, cursor landing, notices, and what carries over on `B`.
- **Store effect**, re-read through the fixture: every `m` flow, with a real `sh` editor for close.
- **Frames**: board modes added to `frameModes` at 80, 120, and 200 columns. They check only that lines fill the frame and are not controls, per `frame_test.go`. No saved snapshot frames.
- **Byte-exact**: a card-render function for the three card lines and the column heading. Card geometry lives in `tui`, as row geometry does.

**TUI controls (`internal/tui/mutations.json`)**
Rule: controls go only on branches the board owns. Where the board calls a flow the list already has (the editor's empty or `:cq` refusal, reopen's `y`, the `r` predicate in `applyFilter`, the stale marker and poll), it gets a test through the board path but no second control. The exception is a board branch that chooses which flow to run.
1. Column derivation, one control per branch: open + ready → Ready; open + blocked → Blocked; in progress + blocked → **In progress**; closed → Closed.
2. Closed order: the board does not re-sort (the order itself is core's).
3. `m` picker rows: the card's own status is left out; Ready and Blocked appear as one `open` row.
4. `m` → in progress calls the start-and-claim write, not `SetIssueStatus`.
5. `m` → closed goes through the editor flow. Leaving Closed goes through the reopen prompt, and only when there is a reason to lose.
6. The "open — blocked by N" status line appears only when the card lands in Blocked.
7. Cursor after a write: it follows its id into the new column; if the card left the view, it goes to the next card, else the previous one, else the nearest non-empty column (three controls).
8. `tab` lands on the nearest row position and wraps around the four columns.
9. Paging: columns shown = max(1, board width ÷ 28), and the focused column scrolls into view from both left and right (two controls).
10. Card and heading: age comes from created, started, or closed depending on the column; each part of line 3 appears only when present; the `39–41` range appears only on overflow; `▸` marks only the focused column.
11. Empty hints: `r to show blocked` appears only under `r` and only in Blocked; `nothing closed` only in Closed.
12. `C` on the board shows its notice and leaves the list's `C` state alone (two controls). Switching with `B` reads nothing and carries the cursor id over.

"The cursor and card stay put after a cancelled close or declined reopen" gets a board-path test but **no control**: the existing refusal controls and the id-tracking control already cover it.

**Core controls (`internal/core/mutations.json`)**
- Start-and-claim: claims only when unclaimed; leaves an existing claim alone; sets `started_at` only once; refuses a tombstoned issue.
- Closed read: `closed_at DESC`; `id` breaks ties; scoped to the project (all projects under `a`); closed issues only, tombstoned left out.
- Live-labels read: tombstoned memberships left out; names sorted.
- Blocker graph read: the "only this blocker" downstream rule still holds when impacts are computed from a map the caller passes in.
- "`OpenBlockers` is read once per refresh" is a cost, not a behaviour. It gets a benchmark or read-count check and is **not** catalogued.

**Out of scope**: a test holding the `?` help screen to the contract's key table. It would be a new doc-sync test for the whole navigator, not something the board needs.

- **Existing narrowings**: what `/` filter and `r` (ready-only) mean on a board — does `r` hide the Blocked column? Is `C` meaningless now that Closed always shows?
- **After a write or refresh**: the cursor rides its tracked id — including into another column after a move — and how ESC-cancelled close restores position.
- **Stale marker and polling**: unchanged, or does a board need anything different?


--- COMMENTS ---
Context from [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3): closing a card uses the `x close` `$EDITOR` flow, not an inline modal, so "ESC-cancelled close" here means an empty reason or `:cq`, and the card goes back to its previous column. Leaving Closed puts up the `reopen` y/N prompt, and a "no" leaves the card in Closed. A move to open can land in Blocked instead of Ready, so the cursor should follow the card's id to whichever column it actually lands in.

--- next comment ---

## Resolution

Board mode inside `drops tui` reuses the navigator's keymap wherever it can. Every existing key keeps its meaning in both modes, with one exception: `C` on the board.

**Entering and leaving**
- `B` toggles between the list and the board. `b` keeps paging the detail pane up.
- `drops tui` always opens in the list. There is **no `--board` flag** in v1.
- **What carries over when you switch**: the cursor's issue id, the `/` filter, `a` scope, `r`, and the follow trail. Switching reads nothing; both views use the loaded rows. The one exception is that the board always includes closed issues (see `C` below).
- `Esc` does **not** leave the board. The board is a view with its own toggle key, like `a`, and not a layer that `Esc` pops.

**Movement**
- Within a column: `j` `k` `↓` `↑` `g` `G` `^d` `^u`.
- Between columns: `tab` / `shift+tab`, cycling through the four. The cursor lands on the card nearest its old row position.
- `h` `l` `←` `→` `0` `$` `J` `K` `space` `b` `w` `enter` `f` `Backspace` `x` `y` all work on the board as they do in the list. Moving the card cursor clears the follow trail, as moving the list cursor does.

**Card moves**
- `m` opens a picker, built like the `x` modal, over the target statuses other than the card's own: `open`, `in progress`, `closed`. Ready and Blocked appear as **one `open` row**. That is how this ticket applies [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3)'s "both columns accept a card": the card lands wherever its readiness puts it, and the status line says why (e.g. "open — blocked by 2").
- The picker then runs the flows that ticket decided: `in progress` claims if unclaimed; `closed` opens the `$EDITOR` flow; leaving Closed asks `reopen`'s y/N.

**Narrowings**
- `/` filters cards in every column, unchanged.
- `r` uses the **same predicate in the same function** (`blockedBy == 0` in `applyFilter`). On the board, Blocked goes empty and shows `r to show blocked`, and blocked In progress cards are hidden too.
- `C` on the board changes nothing and shows the notice `closed always shown on the board`, which clears on the next key, like `y`'s. The board loads closed issues whatever `C` is set to, and the list keeps its own `C` state for when you switch back.

**After a write or refresh**
- The cursor follows its tracked id into whichever column the card lands in.
- A cancelled close (empty reason or `:cq`) or a "no" to reopen writes nothing, so the cursor and card stay where they were.
- If the card leaves the view (tombstoned, filtered out, or hidden by `r` after landing in Blocked), the cursor goes to the next card in the same column, or the previous card if it was the last. If the column is now empty, it goes to the nearest non-empty column. The detail pane then opens the new issue at line 0, following the existing different-issue rule.

**Stale marker and polling**
- No change: the `write_seq` poll runs every 2 seconds, `stale · R` appears on the footer, and `R` refreshes whichever view is up.

# What does the board's contract and test surface look like?
labels: wayfinder:grilling

## Question

With the look, keymap, moves, and reads decided, what does the board add to the documented contract and to the test surface?

- **Contract**: what `docs/cli-contract.md`'s TUI section says about board mode. That covers `B`, the columns and how they're derived, the card, `m` and its flows, `C`'s notice, and `r` emptying Blocked. It also covers whether anything outside the TUI section changes (no new CLI verb, per the map).
- **Boundary tests**: which observable board behaviours get a test against real temp SQLite, and at what level: a frame rendered at a fixed size, the model's state after key messages, or the store effect of a move.
- **Mutation controls**: the load-bearing branches that each need a catalogued control in `internal/tui/mutations.json` and `internal/core/mutations.json`. On the TUI side that includes column derivation (in-progress-and-blocked stays in In progress), the Closed recency order, cursor landing after a move, the cancelled-close and declined-reopen no-ops, and paging the focused column into view. On the core side it covers the new reads and the start-and-claim write decided in [What does moving a card do to status, claim, and close reason?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/3) and [What reads does the board make, and which does core lack?](https://github.com/tedkulp/drops/issues/4).


--- COMMENTS ---
## Resolution

**Contract (`docs/cli-contract.md`)**
- Board mode goes in a new `### The board` subsection at the end of "The navigator: `drops tui`". It adds a `B` row to the key table and one sentence in the intro saying the navigator has two views. The subsection says once that every key keeps its meaning, then lists the exceptions: the derived columns, the 3-line card, `tab`, `m` and its three flows, `C`'s notice, `r` emptying Blocked, where the cursor lands after a write, and paging.
- The rest of the section stays as it is. The `?` help screen and the key table both gain `B`, `tab`, and `m`.
- Outside the TUI section, only **Known rough edges** gets a line: Closed loads with no limit, and a refresh costs about 100ms at around 10k closed issues. No new verb or flag, no census change (`tui` is already registered), and no new exit code. A `CHANGELOG` entry goes under Unreleased → Added.

**Test levels** (all against real temp SQLite)
- **Model state after key messages**: column membership, focused and first visible column, cursor landing, notices, and what carries over on `B`.
- **Store effect**, re-read through the fixture: every `m` flow, with a real `sh` editor for close.
- **Frames**: board modes added to `frameModes` at 80, 120, and 200 columns. They check only that lines fill the frame and are not controls, per `frame_test.go`. No saved snapshot frames.
- **Byte-exact**: a card-render function for the three card lines and the column heading. Card geometry lives in `tui`, as row geometry does.

**TUI controls (`internal/tui/mutations.json`)**
Rule: controls go only on branches the board owns. Where the board calls a flow the list already has (the editor's empty or `:cq` refusal, reopen's `y`, the `r` predicate in `applyFilter`, the stale marker and poll), it gets a test through the board path but no second control. The exception is a board branch that chooses which flow to run.
1. Column derivation, one control per branch: open + ready → Ready; open + blocked → Blocked; in progress + blocked → **In progress**; closed → Closed.
2. Closed order: the board does not re-sort (the order itself is core's).
3. `m` picker rows: the card's own status is left out; Ready and Blocked appear as one `open` row.
4. `m` → in progress calls the start-and-claim write, not `SetIssueStatus`.
5. `m` → closed goes through the editor flow. Leaving Closed goes through the reopen prompt, and only when there is a reason to lose.
6. The "open — blocked by N" status line appears only when the card lands in Blocked.
7. Cursor after a write: it follows its id into the new column; if the card left the view, it goes to the next card, else the previous one, else the nearest non-empty column (three controls).
8. `tab` lands on the nearest row position and wraps around the four columns.
9. Paging: columns shown = max(1, board width ÷ 28), and the focused column scrolls into view from both left and right (two controls).
10. Card and heading: age comes from created, started, or closed depending on the column; each part of line 3 appears only when present; the `39–41` range appears only on overflow; `▸` marks only the focused column.
11. Empty hints: `r to show blocked` appears only under `r` and only in Blocked; `nothing closed` only in Closed.
12. `C` on the board shows its notice and leaves the list's `C` state alone (two controls). Switching with `B` reads nothing and carries the cursor id over.

"The cursor and card stay put after a cancelled close or declined reopen" gets a board-path test but **no control**: the existing refusal controls and the id-tracking control already cover it.

**Core controls (`internal/core/mutations.json`)**
- Start-and-claim: claims only when unclaimed; leaves an existing claim alone; sets `started_at` only once; refuses a tombstoned issue.
- Closed read: `closed_at DESC`; `id` breaks ties; scoped to the project (all projects under `a`); closed issues only, tombstoned left out.
- Live-labels read: tombstoned memberships left out; names sorted.
- Blocker graph read: the "only this blocker" downstream rule still holds when impacts are computed from a map the caller passes in.
- "`OpenBlockers` is read once per refresh" is a cost, not a behaviour. It gets a benchmark or read-count check and is **not** catalogued.

**Out of scope**: a test holding the `?` help screen to the contract's key table. It would be a new doc-sync test for the whole navigator, not something the board needs.
